title: some and any
subtitle: some money / any money
summary: Use some in positive sentences and any in negative sentences and most questions.

left.label: some (positive)
left.text: A woman is smiling. She has notes and coins in her hands: 'I've got **some** money.'

right.label: any (negative)
right.text: A man opens his empty pockets. His wallet is empty too: 'I haven't got **any** money.'
examples: There **isn't any** milk in the fridge.

lesson.heading: any in questions
lesson.text: In most questions (but not all) we use **any**, not *some*.

examples.text: Is there **any** ice in the fridge?

lesson.heading: some in offers and requests
lesson.text: We normally use **some** (not *any*) when we offer things (**Would you like ... ?**) or when we ask for things (**Can I have ... ?**).

examples.text: *A:* Would you like **some** coffee? *B:* Yes, please.
*A:* Can I have **some** soup, please? *B:* Yes. Help yourself.
*A:* Can you lend me **some** money? *B:* Sure. How much do you need?

lesson.heading: some and any without a noun
lesson.text: You can use **some** and **any** alone, without a noun, when we both know what you mean.

examples.text: I didn't take any photographs, but Jane took **some**.
You can have some coffee, but I don't want **any**.
I've just made some coffee. Would you like **some**?
*A:* Where's your luggage? *B:* I haven't got **any**.
*A:* Are there any biscuits? *B:* Yes, there are **some** in the kitchen.

lesson.text: *-body* and *-one* are the same: somebody = someone, anybody = anyone.

exercises.prompt: I'm going to the post office. I need ___ stamps.
exercises.explanation: This is a positive sentence, so we use some.

exercises.prompt: There aren't ___ shops in this part of town.
exercises.explanation: aren't is negative, so we use any.

exercises.prompt: Match each positive sentence with the same sentence in the negative.

pairs.left: I'm going to buy some clothes.
pairs.right: I'm not going to buy any clothes.

pairs.left: There's some ice in the fridge.
pairs.right: There isn't any ice in the fridge.

exercises.prompt: Have you got ___ brothers or sisters?
exercises.explanation: In most questions we use any.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Would you like ___ tea? *B:* Yes, please.
exercises.explanation: We use some when we offer things: Would you like some tea?

exercises.prompt: Does each sentence need some or any?

items.text: There are ___ beautiful flowers in the garden.
Do you know ___ good hotels in London?
When we were on holiday, we visited ___ very interesting places.
Gary and Alice haven't got ___ children.
I went out to buy ___ oranges.
The radio isn't working. There aren't ___ batteries in it.

exercises.prompt: The police want to talk to you. They want to ask you ___.
exercises.explanation: A positive sentence, so: some questions.

exercises.prompt: I haven't got my camera, so I can't take ___.
exercises.explanation: can't is negative, so: any photographs.

exercises.prompt: A woman stopped me and said ___, but I didn't understand.
exercises.explanation: said is positive, so we use something.

exercises.prompt: I'm looking for my keys. Has ___ seen them?
exercises.explanation: In questions we use anybody or anyone.

exercises.statement: This is a secret. Please don't tell somebody.
exercises.explanation: don't tell is negative, so we need anybody: Please don't tell anybody.

exercises.prompt: Jane did not take photographs at the party, but the speaker did. Put the sentence in order.
exercises.answer: Jane didn't take any photographs, but I took some.
exercises.explanation: any after the negative didn't, and some in the positive part.
